content.thinking:
I'm envisioning a fantasy soul scythe displayed life-size, roughly 1.9m tall on a stand or lying flat so it touches the floor—a dragonbone shaft with a curved bone blade featuring a glowing teal-green soul-ethereal edge, styled with League of Legends' exaggerated, dynamic shapes and high-contrast saturated accents.

For the display, I'm thinking of a plinth with a rune ring glow and socketed spike holding the shaft upright, bringing the total height to about 2.2m so the weapon visually touches the floor. Since weapons don't need a full skeleton, I'm planning just a root joint plus maybe a small hinge chain for hanging soul-chain charms or tassels that can swing.

Now I'm figuring out orientation and components: the blade should sweep in the X-Y plane so it reads clearly from a front three-quarter view, with the shaft vertical at the origin. I'm breaking the build into pieces — an octagonal stepped plinth with dragon-claw talons curling up to grip the butt spike, and a dragonbone shaft styled as a spinal column of vertebrae segments following a gentle S-curve.

For the spine, I'm planning vertebra discs spaced with small gaps that reveal a thin glowing teal core running through the center, with spinous and transverse processes as spikes along the bone. The lower grip section gets wrapped dark leather with gold/teal bands and ring guards, the upper section is the exposed vertebra spine, and the head sits at the top where the blade attaches.

I'm settling on a palette of ivory and shadow-bone for the vertebrae, dark iron/obsidian and deep purple for the metal and grip, and a bright soul-teal for the glowing core and accents, keeping gold minimal. For the head, I'm envisioning a dragon skull where the blade curves outward like the dragon's own spine or horn extending into a crescent shape.

The blade itself is forming from a massive curved dragon rib or wing-finger bone, with a thin translucent teal membrane glowing along the inner edge like classic scythe geometry — concave edge, curving so the tip sweeps back toward the shaft. The skull mounts at the top facing forward with jaws open around a glowing soul orb, and the blade sweeps outward from behind it in the horizontal plane.

I'm mapping out the blade's curve with specific coordinates: the shaft top around (0, 1.95), spine arcing outward through a few bezier points to a tip near (1.25, 1.5), giving an overall model height around 2.2m and width 1.4m — oversized but still readable as a scythe. I'm planning to build the blade outline by sampling points along outer and inner curves and extruding between them.

Now I'm thinking through construction: rather than a simple taper extrude, I'll build the spine as a tapering bone-like tube sweep with ridges, and the blade surface as a separate colored membrane between spine and edge lines — dark obsidian-violet with a glowing teal cutting edge, plus layered bone plates along the spine, and etched rune decals painted onto the blade surface.

Computing distance-to-edge gradient for paint...

I'm also layering a glowing edge sweep with flat caps, plus ghostly teal wisp cards rising off the blade edge and floating soul orbs near the skull for extra flavor.

For composition, I'm placing the dragon skull face-on at the shaft's crown with jaws open around a glowing soul orb, the blade rooting into its back via the horns/spine so it reads clearly from the front with the blade extending rightward, balanced by a curved horn or spike as a counterweight on the left.

Pitching it down 15° so the three-quarter and top-down views both read well. I'll build the dragon skull from a cranium ellipsoid, a tapered snout, swept-back brow horns, cheek spikes, and dark eye sockets glowing teal.

I'm planning the jaw as a separate hinged joint so it can rig and open, with the orb sitting between the skull and jaw. For the joint hierarchy, I'm setting up a root base joint, a shaft joint, a head joint at the skull, the jaw hinge, and a three-joint chain for the hanging lantern chain. I'm also adjusting proportions, sizing the skull a bit chunkier at 0.38 long relative to the 2.2m scythe for that stylized look.

Now I'm placing the head joint behind the skull and orienting it to aim forward with a slight downward pitch, using local coordinate helpers (forward/up/right) to position features relative to that joint — keeping in mind that "right" corresponds to the model's negative X axis. For the cranium itself, I'm building it as a scaled, ellipsoid-shaped sphere primitive positioned slightly forward of the head joint, working out how to orient that ellipsoid correctly given the head's pitch.

Actually, simpler to work directly in my own skull frame: build a helper that converts local skull coordinates (x left, y up, z forward) into world points by applying skull origin plus a rotation matrix for the pitch angle about the X axis.

For bones, parts with `bone: head` attach rigidly at the head joint's world position, while lower jaw parts attach similarly at the jaw joint -- both work fine since `at` plus `bone` just pins the part to that joint's transform. I'm working out the rotation math for pitch about the X axis so the orientation quaternion lines up correctly with the geometry axes.

Now I'm defining a skull-local coordinate helper that maps local x/y/z offsets through the pitch quaternion into world space, with mirroring for left/right symmetry. I'm sketching the skull's component layout -- cranium as an ellipsoid, snout built from a series of loft stations in skull-space converted to world coordinates -- figuring out origin placement and radii for each piece.

Now I'm roughing out the remaining skull details: brow ridge sweeps, dark eye sockets with glowing teal spheres inset, nostril bumps, and the start of the horn sweep geometry curving back and out from the brow.

Still placing horn geometry... I'll add ridged texturing with ring bands along the horns and cap the tips, then add jugal cheek spikes angled outward and downward, plus start blocking in the frill/crest sail fins behind the skull.

Working out the teeth now: looping along the snout sides to generate cone spikes with tapering widths, including slightly larger fang spikes partway down each row, while keeping an eye on total part count against the 1000-part budget. Then I'm starting on the lower jaw, setting up the pivot joint and beginning the loft stations from jaw hinge toward the tip.

Reconsidering placement since the upper snout spans that region and would intersect the orb, I'll instead float the soul orb just in front of the snout tip, hovering clear of the mouth with small wisps connecting back toward the jaws.

Now I'm working on the neck connection—adding a bone-and-dark-iron collar with a teal ring just below the skull where it meets the shaft—then figuring out where the blade's spine bone roots into the back-top of the skull.

Plotting out the blade's spine curve rising from the yoke into a tapered bone-like sweep, then working out the concave inner cutting edge from tip back toward the root.

Combining inner and outer points into the final outline polygon, then extruding it flat along a world-aligned plane with slight thickness and bevel to give the blade form. I'm also planning a tapering spine thickness from root to tip with small ridge details along its length.

Adding graduated dorsal spines along the outer edge for a serrated dragon-spine silhouette, plus a thicker tube radius for the spine versus the thin blade for contrast. For coloring, I'm setting up a distance-based gradient from the inner edge outward, going from bright cyan near the edge to teal further in for a glowing, high-contrast blade look.

I'm layering in violet filigree lines at periodic offset distances for engraved detail, and considering teal "soul cracks" in the darker cell regions for extra texture. Since painted surfaces can't actually glow, I'll keep the glow effect separate — a thin emissive sweep along the inner edge plus glowing rune decals overlaid on top.

For the sweep itself, I'm tracing a catmull-rom curve through the inner points with a tapering radius down toward the tip, rendered bright teal where the spine and edge converge. Now I'm also sketching a secondary ghostly echo blade made from layered wisp-card textures — flame-like teardrop shapes with teal gradients and alpha cutouts for the flat card geometry.

Positioning roughly 30 of these cards along the edge sweep, I'm building frames at each point that orient the card faces using a blend of the inward concave normal and an upward lean, with the flow direction guiding how each wisp tilts toward the tip.

I'll leave bend and lean minimal, letting the texture itself carry the curl, with two cross cards giving visibility from both front and side angles. Now I'm thinking about adding floating ghost-soul wisps around the blade's concave curve — small teardrop-shaped faces with dark eye holes and a glowing tail, placed as a few cards orbiting near the captured-soul area.

I'm also reconsidering the blade's orientation for top-down readability — a vertical blade plane would look like a thin line from above, so I'm weighing whether real scythe geometry tilts the blade plane relative to the shaft to stay visible from multiple angles.

I consider tilting the blade plane around different axes but none give a clean readable silhouette without distortion, so I'll drop that idea and just keep the scythe standing vertical on its plinth.

For the shaft, I'm designing a gentle S-curve path rather than a perfectly straight line, using a subtle sine offset that returns to zero at both ends so the skull stays centered at the top. I'm working out how to orient the vertebrae segments along this curved path using tangent frames so each part follows the shaft's direction naturally.

Now I'm laying out the shaft's regions from bottom to top: a bone spike or dark iron cap at the base, a long leather-wrapped grip section with spiral teal thread and bone ring spacers, then a guard ring area where I'm considering a carved bone bulb or dragon claw cluster as a central ornamental feature.

For palette, I'm settling on spectral teal as the single strong accent, with bone ivory, deep violet-black, and sparing antique gold trim for contrast, keeping the total color count low. Above the guard, I'm planning a vertebra-like spine of waisted lathe discs stacked with small gaps between them to suggest a dragonbone motif.

Now I'm working out roughly sixteen vertebrae along the 1.0–1.85 segment, tapering slightly from thicker at the base to narrower near the top, alternating spinous spikes front and back with small transverse wings on the sides, and running a glowing teal core tube through the visible gaps between discs. I'm also noting a thin dark core tube for the lower grip section, with a bone collar and skull form planned at the top around 1.86.

Then I'm adding a hanging charm from a ring near y 0.95 -- a short hinge-jointed chain of three links leading down to a small lantern gem caged in bone, plus a couple of bone beads and a tasseled ribbon card dangling alongside it for decoration.

For the base, I'm designing an octagonal plinth of dark violet stone with scale textures and a cracked finish, topped with a glowing rune-ring decal; four tapered dragon claws sweep up from the plinth's rim to grip the shaft near y .4, each with dark knuckle joints, and the shaft seats into a socket collar at the plinth's center so the whole piece touches the floor properly.

I'm adding small decorative touches too: scattered bone fragments or coins, a handful of glowing teal crystal shards shaped as hexagonal prisms around the plinth edge, and faint rising wisp motifs, all tied together by the painted rune ring on top.

Now I'm figuring out the rune ring placement as a thin flat decal positioned on the plinth's upper step, sized to fit the narrow radius band between the step edges so the glowing teal runes sit visibly on the flat surface facing upward.

I'll add that floor decal at y=0.003 for top-down readability, a thin glowing teal magic circle, but need to check it doesn't push the overall bounding width too wide — maybe scale it down to radius 0.85 since the scythe itself is already about 1.4m wide.

Actually I realize the asymmetry is a problem: the blade extends far to +X while the shaft/plinth sit near x=0, so the whole model's center of mass is off-balance. I should shift the shaft and plinth to roughly x=-0.4 so the blade tip and the base counterbalance each other and the composition reads as centered on x=0.

Rather than translating fully-constructed parts, I'll define a global offset constant and build a small helper function that applies it to every literal world-space point I place, so all pieces stay consistently shifted without touching joint-local logic.

Checking the bounding box after the shift, the floor ring becomes asymmetric around the shaft, so I'll shrink the plinth and floor ring radii to keep things tidy. Total height works out to roughly 2.35 units with the blade and spines included, which is reasonable for a fantasy-scaled greatscythe around 2.2-2.3 meters tall.

Now I'm planning the glow palette—teal as the primary accent with a violet secondary for darker iron materials, and defining mottled paint helpers for the bone texture using light and dark bone tones.

For larger bone pieces like the skull, I want a hand-painted countershading effect: a mottled base with a darker gradient toward the bottom, giving that layered painted-shadow look common in LoL/Blizzard style assets. All painted surfaces will share a single texture sheet for efficiency.

For the shaft wrap, I'm calculating a spiral stripe pattern for the leather grip — working out turn counts based on wrap length and stripe spacing to generate alternating color bands, plus a plain dark leather variant with a thin teal thread accent. Now I'm starting to tally up the full parts list (aiming for around 500 pieces), starting with the plinth components like the base lathe and rune plane.

Continuing the inventory, I'm adding the claws (sweeps, knuckle spheres, nails), crystals, and bone-spike studs around the plinth rim, then moving down the shaft to plan the butt cap, grip sweep, gold ring bands, bone spacers, and thread detail, followed by the guard ornament with its ring and radial bone talon spikes, and finally the spine's repeating vertebrae structure with transverse processes, spinous bumps, and glow rings leading up to the collar.

Now I'm working through the skull, blade, and spine details: counting roughly 70 parts for the skull, then planning the blade's extrude, edge glow, spine sweep, spiked ridges, gold ferrule bands, and the iron root yoke with claws gripping it. I'm also figuring out how to add rune decals onto the curved blade surface -- since a flat decal rectangle won't follow the curve, I'm considering placing small rune-stamped planes along the blade's midline, each rotated to match the local tangent, and applying them to both faces so the runes are visible from front and back.

I'm defining how each rune plane is oriented using the curve tangent as its up vector, so the glyphs roll naturally along the blade's curvature, with glowing variants spread across both sides using a handful of distinct glyph textures. I'm also sketching in extra bone-like ridges fanning from the spine toward the edge on both faces, like wing struts, using tapered rods with bone coloring to add texture and richness, then checking how this interacts with the edge zone before moving on to wisp card placement along the edge.

Now I'm working out the blade's geometry mathematically — defining the spine and outer path as control points in design space sampled along a curve, then computing the inward normal from the tangent direction so I can offset the inner edge correctly as the blade curves from the root outward to its downward-curling tip.

I should add a minimum width near the root so it's not zero, but need to check the inner edge doesn't collide with the skull/collar geometry since they occupy similar z-depth near the base.

I'm also considering adding a few jagged notches along the inner edge to give the blade a "soul-cutting" serrated look, using a sawtooth modulation of the offset width at a few points along the curve rather than a smooth taper.

I think I'll skip serration on the glow itself and instead let the glow trace a smoothed version of the spiky polyline, keeping the sharp corners only on the solid shape.

I'm deciding against serration for a cleaner look, opting instead for simple outer spines and a few gentle scallops along the inner edge between the rib struts, using a subtle width modulation to create that soft wave effect.

Thinking about the scallop direction more—making the edges bulge outward convex with inward cusps so it reads like a bat-wing membrane, with concave bites between pointed teeth rather than smooth bumps.

Now I'm adding bone-colored ribs running from spine to each cusp point on both faces, raised slightly off the blade surface, tapered rods partially embedded into the thickness. I'm also setting up a function to measure distance from paint points to the blade edge, sampling the outline polyline densely for accuracy.

Writing distance calculation code...

I'm defining the blade's edge-lit color gradient — teal darkening into indigo based on distance from the edge, with fine engraved lines etched in at specific distances and noise-based mottling for organic variation, applying the same scheme to the extruded side walls.

Checking texel density across the shared 1024 paint sheet given the total painted surface area, I bump the paint resolution to 2048 for crisper engraving lines, keeping the atlas at 4096 to accommodate it. Now I'm moving on to building small SVG rune glyph textures with teal stroke paths for the glow elements.

I'm sketching the rest of the glow texture set: a plinth rune ring generated procedurally with repeated glyph strokes around a circle, a floor magic circle with thin circles, triangles, and dots sized for clean stroke widths, plus flame and ghost-soul textures for the wisp and spirit effects. For materials, I confirm the textured glow planes only need front-face rendering, and I'm positioning the floor ring plane just above the base, extending outward past the plinth itself.

I'm working out the soul orb design -- a small teal core sphere surrounded by thin torus-shaped orbit rings for a glowing halo effect, with wisp cards floating around it. I'm also considering a hanging charm made of gold chain links with hinge joints, checking whether the chain builder supports a "hinge" role and how parenting should work for that joint.

For the chain itself, I'm sketching a path hanging straight down with a gold bail ring at the top and a gem lantern at the tip, built from a stretched octahedron shape with a teal glow.

I'm working out the joint hierarchy: a root "base" joint, then a "shaft" joint parented to it, with the head and chain joints branching off further down. I'll assign bones explicitly to each part rather than relying on proximity, keeping plinth pieces at base and everything else at shaft.

I'm sketching helper utilities for placing geometry in world space, defining a coordinate type and a small offset function, and limiting myself to a modest flat color palette for the paints.

Now I'm working out a skull frame transform with a slight downward pitch, then double-checking the sign of the rotation matrix for the x-axis to make sure the tilt goes the right direction.

I'm defining helper functions for orienting parts and spikes with the skull's local quaternion, and setting up an ellipsoid-part helper that builds scaled sphere geometry at given skull-local coordinates, checking whether non-uniform scaling plays nicely with normals in the exporter.

Now I'm sketching the actual skull anatomy: cranium and occipital ellipsoids positioned relative to the head bone, brow ridges built from tapered capsule sweeps, and starting the snout as a lofted shape.

Continuing the snout loft with tapering stations toward the tip, then adding the nose bump, dark nostril ellipsoids, and eye socket cavities using dark coloring to carve out depth before placing the glowing eyes.

Adding a teal eye glow nestled in the socket with brow overhang, then placing flat jugal cheek plates and backward-pointing spikes for the skull's rugged profile, plus a small gold-toned sphere marking the jaw hinge.

Now I'm sweeping horn geometry with painted ring bands alternating light and dark along their length, curving them outward then upward and back in a lateral sweep — though I'm noticing the horn tip position might collide with the blade root attached above on the same side.

I'm checking the coordinates more carefully: the horn tip lands dangerously close to the blade spine's path, with only a tiny z-gap separating them around the same x,y region. To avoid this, I'm adjusting the horn curve so it sweeps outward and back with only a slight upturn instead of curling sharply upward, pulling it away from the spine's trajectory.

Now I'm also sketching a smaller crest structure — three spikes running along the midline of the skull, each pointing upward with slightly varying heights and depth positions to give the crest some natural irregularity.

Then I shift to the teeth: seven upper teeth per side spaced along the jaw, tapering in width toward the back, each generated as a downward-pointing spike whose direction follows the skull's rotation so they angle correctly in world space.

For the lower jaw, I'm defining its bone with a joint and aim target, then setting up loft stations that taper from a wide base near the chin down to a narrower tip toward the back, with upward-pointing spikes forming the lower teeth row.

I'm placing six smaller teeth per side plus two larger upward-curving fangs further back, adding a tiny chin spike, and giving the mouth interior a glowing teal tongue slab to simulate soul-fire light visible when the jaw opens.

Now I'm setting up the jaw rotation using a positive 24-degree pivot around the model's X-axis, confirming that this tips the forward-pointing jaw bone downward as intended, and checking that the lower jaw tip drops roughly .12m from its pivot point once opened.

I'm placing the orb in front of the open mouth around SK(0,-.07,.44), proportionate to the skull's overall length. Then I work out the neck connection, sweeping a thickened bone from the underside of the skull down to the shaft at W(0,1.84), adding a slight S-curve so it reads as natural dragon neck vertebrae continuing the spine before planning the shaft's vertebrae path from W(0,1.0) up to W(0,1.86).

Writing vertebra geometry...

I'll simplify: a dorsal spine on every vertebra with sideways transverse processes extruding left and right for a wing-like silhouette, plus a glowing flat disc between vertebrae for the core ring effect.

Working out the glow tube's sizing so it sits flush with the vertebra edges in the gaps rather than poking through, settling on a slightly larger radius to make it visible as a clean ring.

Now I'm planning the lower shaft: the leather-wrapped grip section with its taper radius, gold lathe bands spiraling down with teal inlay threads, an iron collar and ferrule at the socket end, and a dark iron knuckle guard ring near the top of the grip where it meets the vertebrae.

I'm also designing four bone claws emerging from that knuckle ring, curving downward and outward like talons gripping the shaft, with tapering radii from base to point and gold accents, plus four larger claws rising from the plinth rim to grasp higher up the shaft in a similar talon-like sweep.

Now I'm adding smaller decorative spikes between the main claws, and placing six teal crystal shards around the plinth's base on the floor as glowing accents, using octahedron geometry for each shard with slight tilts for variation.

I'm also adding wispy teal ghost flame cards rising from the plinth rim at several points, plus a handful of floating ghost cards nearby, and planning rune planes and an edge glow sweep along the blade's spine using a tube swept along the edge polyline.

Now I'm placing small glowing teal gem studs along the spine between the spikes on the front and back faces, computing their positions by offsetting outward along z based on a tapering radius function that shrinks from root to tip.

For the spines themselves, I'm having them point outward along the surface normal with a slight tangent bend toward the tip, spacing nine spikes along the spine's length with sizes that peak in the middle and taper at the ends, colored to match bone. I'm also adding an iron mounting clamp around the spine's root, building it as a lathed ring shape oriented along the spine's tangent direction.

Now I'm bridging the spine's base to the neck vertebra with a thick iron capsule shape, since the spine starts offset slightly behind and above the neck joint.

I'm laying out the curved spine path using a sequence of control points with catmull-rom interpolation, then checking whether the blade's width near the root overlaps the skull's bounding region in x, y, and z before settling on a tapering width function along the curve.

No actual collision then—the blade root acts like a backing plate behind the skull, similar to a frill. I'll tweak the width falloff curve so it doesn't bulge too much near the root, and plan to build the outline by tracing outer points forward then inner points in reverse, merging at the tip so the two edges meet cleanly with zero width.

For the actual geometry, the outline needs to sit in local coordinates relative to the extrude anchor, with enough points (around 96) to capture the scalloped edge without exceeding limits or self-intersecting. I'll skip extra smoothing since detail is already fine, and just use a small bevel. Writing scallop edge logic...

Working out scallop alignment so cusps land on index 8 plus multiples of 8, skipping smoothing for the early indices, then setting up the glow edge as a matching 3D polyline using the inner points.

For the edge tube, a radius of .009 against the .022 extrude thickness keeps it nearly flush while still forming a bright glowing cutting line, and I'm considering whether a thin parallel glow line is also needed alongside the edge. For blade runes, I'm placing glyphs at several stations along the curve offset toward the edge, varying the glyph type by index.

Placing glyphs on both front and back faces with matching orientation so the back reads correctly without mirroring, since the plane's axes naturally flip with the normal direction. I'm staggering rune positions so they land between rib cusps instead of overlapping them, giving six runes per face spaced across the blade.

Now I'm defining the ribs: each one runs from an outer spine point to an inner cusp point, slightly offset inward on both faces, with tapered rod radii colored bone, skipping the tip rib since its width goes to zero. I'm also setting up the tapered spine sweep path with a radius function that shrinks from base to tip, paired with bone-colored paint.

For the paint pattern, I'm adding periodic darker seam stripes along the spine to mimic vertebral segments—dividing the length into roughly 34 bands and marking a thin dark line at the start of each one against a mottled bone base, giving the tail a segmented vertebrae look.

Now I'm moving on to the glyph SVGs: using a 64x64 viewBox at 128px size with rounded teal strokes, starting with the first glyph's path data.

I'm sketching out the remaining glyphs—a circle crossed by perpendicular lines, a triangular peak with a crossbar, and an hourglass-like shape with a dot—all using round-capped strokes and a glowing teal color so they read as mystical icon marks against a transparent background.

Then I move to designing a ring-shaped plinth using a larger 200x200 viewBox, mapping the ring's inner and outer radii proportionally to the plane's physical dimensions so it scales correctly.

Writing ring and glyph SVG...

I'm also laying out a floor circle design with concentric rings, a dashed inner ring, and a rotated hexagram-like polygon of points, keeping stroke widths scaled so they render crisply at the target raster size.

Writing wisp flame SVG...

Now I'm sketching a ghost sprite with a rounded body shape and scalloped bottom edges, and figuring out how to carve eye holes using an evenodd fill rule within the same path rather than separate cutout shapes.

I should feed the card meshes from b.cards into the glow function directly since it accepts arrays of meshes, keeping texture colors as-is without extra tinting. Now I'm defining the color palette constants, starting with a bone tone.

Still defining the color palette...

Writing plinth cracks shader...

For the blade, I'm computing distance to the nearest polyline segment across the cutting edge, then coloring by proximity: near-white at the very edge, teal glow just beyond, fading into darker teal further out.

Then I'm adding engraved rib lines at fixed distances and crack-like fractures using cellular noise, dimmed teal against the dark base, plus subtle mottling for texture. The walls and bevels reuse this same paint, while bone ribs and plinth shards get their own treatment, and I'm now thinking about where to place cards and ghost positions within the blade's concave region.

Placing floating ghosts near the inner curve of the blade, treating them as unattached elements that can hover loosely rather than being tied to the geometry. I'm also considering exaggerating the skull and blade for a stylized, dynamic silhouette.

I'm adding gold filigree details on the iron yoke and horn bands, with teal accents woven throughout the eyes, edges, core, orbs, runes, and ghosts for consistency. Now I'm sketching a bone-claw guard at the mid-shaft, with claws radiating outward and downward from a central ring using curved spike geometry.

I'm also working out where to hang a charm from the guard, tracing a chain path downward from a gold eyelet at the front, while checking that the claw spikes at 45° angles don't collide with the chain's position.

For the charm itself, I'm designing a glowing octagonal gem lantern with a tapered gold cap and a tassel made from small hanging card-like spikes.

Now I'm working out the chain bone attachment: setting the charm's parent to the shaft joint and using a catmull-sweep path with typed point arrays to build the chain geometry, matching the names array to the number of spans between points.

I'm defining the base and shaft joints, checking part counts (cards sharing one texture get merged into a single part), and verifying floor contact so nothing sinks below the ground plane except a small acceptable margin. Now I'm setting up imports for the build, making sure I only include the helpers actually used like frame and aim, before writing the final code.

Writing imports and setup...

Still defining joints...

I need to double check types for color, Joint, scale, and quat by grepping the builder source for their exact export signatures before using them.

input.command: ls samples | head -3; ls kits; mkdir -p scratch/soulScytheSonnet; grep -n "scale?" src/builder.ts | head; grep -n "quat?" src/builder.ts | head -5
